The fog did not roll in; it arrived with the weight of a decision. It pressed against the glass of the lantern room, a thick, gray wool that muffled the world until only the rhythmic *thrum-click* of the Fresnel lens remained.

Elias Thorne stood before the great prism, his hand resting on the cold brass railing. He was not young, though age in the isolation of the Farallon Light Station had become a fluid concept. His skin was mapped with the salt-spray wrinkles of a man who had spent forty years looking out at the horizon, and his eyes were the color of the deep sea—dark, shifting, and unreadable.

They called him Lighthouse Keeper #0.

The official logs listed him as Elias Thorne, Senior Keeper, appointed in 1954. But the ships that dared to navigate the treacherous waters off the coast of Oregon knew him by a different designation. Before him, there had been a series of keepers who lasted weeks, then months, before being relieved or resigning in hysterical confusion. There was no Keeper #1, #2, or #3 in the maritime records. Those names had been scrubbed from the ledgers, redacted by men in dark suits who claimed bureaucratic errors.

Elias was the first. He was also the last. Or so it seemed.

The light rotated above him, a mechanical heart beating in time with the tide. *Flash. Darkness. Flash. Darkness.* It was a binary code, a rhythm that had kept sailors alive since 1890. But Elias knew something the captains did not. The light was not just a warning; it was a lock.

The fog didn’t just roll in; it arrived with the weight of a physical presence, pressing against the glass of the lantern room like a curious, cold giant. Inside, Elias Thorne adjusted the wick of the primary lamp, his movements precise, ritualistic, and devoid of hesitation. He was the Keeper of Blackwood Point, though the official logs listed him as "Station Operator #0."

There was no one before him. There had never been a Keeper #1, or #2, or any number up to ninety-nine. The previous administration had burned the archives during the Great Reorganization of 1974, claiming that "legacy data corrupted operational efficiency." They replaced names with numbers. They replaced history with protocols. Elias was the first and only entry in the new ledger. He was #0.

The number zero meant nothing. It meant void. It meant a starting point that had already been passed. Or, as Elias sometimes whispered to the gulls circling the tower, it meant the absence of everything else.

Blackwood Point was not merely a lighthouse; it was a scar on the coastline of Maine, jutting out into the Atlantic like a broken finger. The structure itself was an anomaly—a brutalist concrete cylinder topped with a Victorian glass lantern, a architectural mismatch that mirrored the confusion of its staff. There were no other buildings nearby. No keeper’s quarters for families, no supply sheds, no radio tower. Just the tower, the light, and the sea.
